headline: Widest edge of the season lights up yellowfin at the Washington wall
subhead: A post-blow shelf break pushed the temperature differential to 10.3°F this week — the sharpest structural setup we've seen all year, and the fish know it.
body_markdown:
Last week's blow did what blows always do out here — it stirred the pot and then walked away, leaving something better behind. We had two days of sloppy swell and a hard NE push that shut the door on running offshore, but that same wind did the real work underneath the surface. It sharpened the shelf-slope break to 10.3 degrees Fahrenheit — the widest thermal edge I've measured all season — and it stacked cold upwelled water against the warm Gulf Stream filament sitting on the 100-fathom line. That's the kind of contrast that concentrates bait, and bait concentrates everything else. The same NE flow tightened up the 20 to 30 fathom breaks midshore, which is why the Coimbra corridor at 20 fathoms has bluefin stacked on it right now — smaller class fish, but plenty of them, and they're there because the upwelling pinned sand eels and squid against that break like a wall.

This week the moon's sliding toward new — dark by the 13th or 14th — which means less light on the surface at night and better squid marks under the boat. That's not a small thing out here. A darkening moon is when the overnight squid-light game gets serious: run the generator, hang the greenstick lights over the transom, and let the squid climb the water column into your Sabiki. If you can put fresh squid in the well before sunrise, you're fishing with better bait than ninety percent of the fleet, and on a bite this edge-dependent, bait quality is the difference between a two-fish day and a six-fish day. Tides aren't the driver out here the way they are inshore — it's the thermal structure and the moon-driven light levels that matter most this week.

The bite itself has been good, not great, and I want to be straight about that. Wednesday and Thursday were the best window we've had all season — the warm seam running from Wilmington down through Poor Man's, and the same signature showing up on our own west wall in 280 to 320 fathoms, produced yellowfin in the 35 to 55 pound class trolling a small spread of Green Machines and naked ballyhoo at 6 to 7 knots, working the temp break itself rather than blasting straight across it. The fish were sitting right on the color change — you could see it, dirty green water butting up against a cleaner blue edge — and every strike came within fifty yards of that line. Chunking behind the troll once we found the school put a few more in the box on butterflied bunker, but it wasn't a stack-and-load bite. More like find the edge, get two or three, watch it go quiet, move a half mile down the wall, find it again.

Bluefin have been the more consistent fish this week, and they're shallower than you'd think. The Coimbra corridor at 20 fathoms has had schools of 40 to 60 pound bluefin working bait balls on the surface mid-morning — small, fast-moving spreads with cedar plugs and green-and-yellow Ilanders in daylight, then the light game overnight once you anchor up or drift on the squid. That midshore bite is worth the shorter run if the canyon proper isn't cooperating, and this week it's been the more reliable of the two.

Wahoo have been a bycatch story so far — a couple came off high-speed spreads run wide off the wake in 400-plus fathoms south toward the Baltimore fingers, but nobody's targeting them yet with real intent. Mahi have shown around any floating structure or weed line we crossed running out — a few schoolies in the 5 to 12 pound range around a lobster pot ball southeast of the canyon mouth, worth a stop if you see anything floating, but not a fishery you'd plan a whole trip around right now.

White marlin is the one I'm watching hardest. The warm plume that's been building on the bank is the trigger everyone's waiting for, and the oceanography says we're 7 to 10 days out from the first real flags at the mid-Atlantic canyons. I'd have the dredge rigged and ready on any trip from here forward — better to be a week early with ballyhoo dredges soaking than a week late scrambling to re-rig on the ride out.

If I had one trip to make this week, I'd run Wednesday or Thursday if the wind allows, straight to the warm seam on the west wall, work the color change with a small troll spread, and keep squid gear rigged for an overnight anchor-up on the dark moon if the yellowfin bite is slow. Best case, that 10.3-degree break holds through the weekend and the yellowfin stack tighter on it. If it slides or collapses like these things sometimes do, I'd pivot inshore to the Coimbra bluefin — twenty fathoms of water and a reliable morning bite beats a long run to a wall that's gone quiet.
